notes: NC State has no official university-wide AI policy (DELTA says so as of May 2026). No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred. The student page and DELTA article are guidance, not binding policy. The graduate handbook covers theses and dissertations only. Several units are instructor-directed prompts (DELTA questions to consider), coded with modality may/should and unit_stance neutral. Reconciled with coder B, who found the same three documents and no other layers. Sample statements in the DELTA article are coded with the student as actor even though the document is instructor guidance.

documents.title: AI for Students
documents.summary: Student-facing AI Hub page with study tips for using AI as a search, summary and study aid. It says policies differ by instructor and tells students to ask when unsure.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own: "AI usage policies differ between instructors, courses and assignments" and "Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!" hand the decision to instructors, while only encouraging experimentation within academic policies.

units.why: Tells students to "Experiment extensively with AI tools to learn and solve problems", so AI exploration is welcomed by default for learning; P02 fits since it encourages use, with the policy-compliance clause coded separately.
units.anchor: Experiment extensively with AI tools to learn and solve problems
units.fit_note: Encouragement is qualified by keeping NC State academic policies in mind.

units.why: "keeping NC State academic policies and procedures in mind" ties AI use to existing university rules; P77 (comply with existing policy) fits, not P45 which treats AI as a collaborator.
units.anchor: keeping NC State academic policies and procedures in mind
units.policy: Students keep NC State academic policies and procedures in mind when using AI tools.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: 'Experiment extensively with AI tools to learn and solve problems while keeping NC State academic policies and procedures in mind.' Only B coded the second clause separately. It is a separate rule (stay within existing academic policies), so it is kept as P77. Coder A treated it only as a qualification in the fit note of the first unit.

units.why: "Know which tools are available and which tools are not" points students to the university approved/rejected tool list; closest is vetted-tool preference (P50), though no data rationale is given.
units.anchor: Know which tools are available and which tools are not.
units.fit_note: Only says to know the approved and rejected tools; no mention of data protection. | The type is about data protection; this unit only says to know which university-approved tools are available.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A='general' B='before-course'). Source: 'As students explore university-approved AI tools and solutions, they should: Know which tools are available and which tools are not.' Students are the actors and no course or policy set-up is being done, so the phase is the general orientation to tools (A), not before-course (B). Both coders agree on P50 with a partial-fit note: the line says only to know approved and rejected tools.

units.why: "Focus on familiar subjects to better understand AI strengths and weaknesses" is advice on how to learn about AI; it matches no type, so UNCOVERED. Reconciled coding: phase=during-work.
units.anchor: Focus on familiar subjects to better understand AI’s strengths and weaknesses.
units.uncovered_note: Advice to test AI on familiar subjects to learn its strengths and weaknesses. | (coder B, coded P31) Advises practicing on familiar subjects so students can spot AI strengths and weaknesses, rather than saying to verify output.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A='general' B='during-work'; policy_type: A='UNCOVERED' B='P31'; unit_stance: A='encourage' B='neutral'). Source: 'Focus on familiar subjects to better understand AI's strengths and weaknesses.' A coded UNCOVERED, B coded P31 (verify output). The line advises students to try AI on subjects they know so they can calibrate it; it does not tell them to check output, so P31 would be a stretched fit and UNCOVERED is kept. Phase is during-work because it is advice on how to use the tool.

units.why: "Many scholarly sources and current academic journals are missing from the tool's datasets" is a caution about AI as a search tool; it warns of unreliable output, closest to P31.
units.anchor: Many scholarly sources and current academic journals are missing from the tool's datasets.
units.fit_note: States a limitation (missing scholarly sources) as fact rather than telling students to verify.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: 'Limited Data: Many scholarly sources and current academic journals are missing from the tool's datasets.' Only B coded this. It is a stated limitation that supports the caution to verify output, so it is kept as P31 informs with B's partial-fit note.

units.why: "The tool cannot critically evaluate information or distinguish reliable sources" warns that chatbots lack understanding; fits P31 as a reason to evaluate output critically.
units.anchor: The tool cannot critically evaluate information or distinguish reliable sources.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: 'Lack of True Understanding: The tool cannot critically evaluate information or distinguish reliable sources.' Only B coded this. It is a stated limitation behind the caution to verify output, so it is kept as P31 informs.

units.why: "rely on them with caution" followed by limited data, no true understanding and hallucination risk tells students to treat AI search output skeptically, which is P31.
units.anchor: rely on them with caution
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. Source: 'AI chatbots can provide quick overviews of many topics. However, rely on them with caution.' Only A coded the caution. It is a real recommendation and fits P31 (verify AI output) as a general caution; B coded only the three listed limitations.

units.why: "Be aware of the tool tendency to invent information" names hallucination, so students must verify (P31).
units.anchor: Be aware of the tool’s tendency to invent information.

A coded P32 (student stays the active problem-solver), B coded P12 (AI as tutor for understanding concepts). The point of the line is not to passively accept AI output, which matches P32; AI here is a discussion partner rather than a tutor explaining concepts. P32 kept with A's fit note, which also notes the specific recommended use.

units.anchor: Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A='course-start' B='during-work'). Source: 'Clarify with the Instructor: Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!' A coded course-start, B during-work. The advice applies at the moment a student is deciding whether to use AI on work, so during-work. P10 (ask when unsure) fits and both coders agree on it.

documents.title: Developing Course AI Guidelines & Driving Class AI Discussion
documents.summary: DELTA article for instructors on writing course and assignment AI statements, with three sample statements, questions to consider and discussion activities. It states there is no official university AI policy.
documents.stance_why: The page says "there is no official university policy regarding AI use" and tells instructors to write their own course- and assignment-level guidelines. It offers three sample statements spanning restrictive to collaborative, so it sets tiers/templates and the stance is delegates.

A coded before-course, B course-start. Giving students directions is communicating expectations, so course-start. documents.unit: Graduate School Handbook 3.6 Theses and Dissertations
documents.title: Graduate Handbook: Artificial Intelligence Policy for Dissertations and Theses
documents.summary: Graduate Handbook section on AI in theses and dissertations, plus the authorship statement requirement. It allows generative AI use with required documentation and discusses privacy, bias and detectors.
documents.stance_why: The section says "The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism" and its guiding principle is that candidates "must document their use clearly and thoroughly", so AI is allowed for theses and dissertations on condition of disclosure.

units.why: "propose a framework to allow our graduate students to use these tools ethically" states the purpose of the section (P56).
units.anchor: propose a framework to allow our graduate students to use these tools ethically

units.why: "calculators for words" frames LLMs by analogy with calculators; no type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: LLMs are sometimes described as “calculators for words”
units.uncovered_note: Frames LLMs as calculators for words to set a tone for acceptance of use.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. Source: 'LLMs are sometimes described as calculators for words.' Only A coded this. It is a framing sentence that sets the tone of acceptance for the policy. It is rationale about AI use, and no type covers an analogy used as a rationale, so it is kept as UNCOVERED with A's note.

units.why: "Our students would benefit from receiving training on how to use GAI tools" states a Graduate School position favoring AI training (P70).
units.anchor: Our students would benefit from receiving training on how to use GAI tools efficiently, ethically
units.fit_note: A stated belief that students would benefit; no training is announced.

units.why: "The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism" says use alone is not misconduct; nearest P36, which it negates. Reconciled coding: actor=all.
units.anchor: The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism
units.fit_note: Says mere use is not plagiarism, the opposite of classifying use as misconduct.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A='student' B='all'; policy_type: A='P36' B='P62'). Source: 'The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism.' A coded P36 with actor student, B coded P62 with actor all. The sentence addresses how use is classified (plagiarism), which is P36 (A's fit note says it is the opposite of classifying use as misconduct); it is a Graduate School position for everyone and not only students, so actor all (B). Both code unit_stance permit.

units.why: "the uninformed and/or poorly documented inclusion of outputs from LLMs into dissertations and theses may constitute a form of plagiarism" classes poorly documented AI use as plagiarism: P36.
units.anchor: poorly documented inclusion of outputs from LLMs into dissertations and theses may constitute a form
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (policy_type: A='P28' B='P36'). Source: 'the uninformed and/or poorly documented inclusion of outputs from LLMs into dissertations and theses may constitute a form of plagiarism.' A coded P28 (nondisclosure is the violation), B coded P36 (misconduct). The passage classifies poor documentation as plagiarism, so P36 (the type that names plagiarism) is kept; A's disclosure link is kept in the topics. Both code unit_stance restrict.

units.why: "Candidates utilizing GAI tools must document their use clearly and thoroughly in their dissertation or thesis" is the Graduate School's guiding disclosure rule: P24.
units.anchor: Candidates utilizing GAI tools must document their use clearly and thoroughly in their dissertation or
units.fit_note: Applies to dissertations and theses only.

units.why: "discuss ... acceptable use of LLMs or other GAI tools as early as practically possible with their advisor" is an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: discuss general authorship principles and issues as well as acceptable use of LLMs
units.fit_note: Asks for an early discussion with the advisor, not only when unsure.

units.why: "Advisors need to be direct and transparent about what tools students are permitted to use, and about the reasons" requires advisors to state rules and reasons; nearest P66. Reconciled coding: phase=course-start.
units.anchor: Advisors need to be direct and transparent about what tools students are permitted to use
units.fit_note: Also covers stating which tools are permitted, not only explaining reasons. | (coder B, coded P09) Applies to advisors of theses, not to syllabi, and also asks for reasons (P66).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A='before-course' B='course-start'; policy_type: A='P66' B='P09'). Source: 'Advisors need to be direct and transparent about what tools students are permitted to use, and about the reasons for any restrictions.' A coded P66 before-course, B coded P09 course-start. The line asks advisors to tell students the reasons for restrictions, which P66 covers, and P09 is a syllabus statement, which does not apply to a thesis advisor. Phase is course-start because it is about communicating expectations to students.

units.why: Program rules, "if such principles are adopted by the program, they must be clearly communicated to the students and applied uniformly by advisory committees", add program-level rules that must be communicated: P09.
units.anchor: they must be clearly communicated to the students and applied uniformly by advisory committees
units.fit_note: Concerns program-level principles and uniform application, not a syllabus statement. | Also requires uniform application of program-level principles by advisory committees.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A='before-course' B='course-start'). Source: 'if such principles are adopted by the program, they must be clearly communicated to the students and applied uniformly by advisory committees.' A coded phase before-course, B course-start. Communicating principles to students is communicating expectations, so course-start (B). Both coders agree on P09, with fit notes that it is a program rule about uniform application and not a syllabus statement; the notes are kept.

units.why: "GAI tools raise issues of privacy and intellectual property" names privacy and IP concerns with AI tools: P50.
units.anchor: GAI tools raise issues of privacy and intellectual property.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: 'GAI tools raise issues of privacy and intellectual property.' Only B coded this. It states the concern behind the next sentence about submitted material becoming part of the tool's database, so it is kept as P50 informs.

units.why: "Material submitted can become part of the application database" warns of privacy and IP risks (P50).
units.anchor: Material submitted can become part of the application’s database

units.why: "inherent biases associated with them. Users must, at a minimum, be aware" requires awareness of bias (P53).
units.anchor: Users must, at a minimum, be aware of the existence of such issues.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (modality: A='must' B='should'). Source: 'Users must, at a minimum, be aware of the existence of such issues.' A coded must, B should. The source says 'must', so must (A). Both code P53.

units.why: "the use of AI tools claiming to detect LLM generated text is discouraged" rejects detectors due to unreliability (P39).
units.anchor: the use of AI tools claiming to detect LLM generated text is discouraged

units.why: "no LLM tool should be credited as co-author on a research paper" is a research authorship rule (P62).
units.anchor: no LLM tool should be credited as co-author on a research paper
units.fit_note: Adds the reason: AI tools cannot take accountability for the work.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A='general' B='during-work'). Source: 'The guidelines from Nature also state that no LLM tool should be credited as co-author on a research paper. That is because any attribution of authorship carries with it accountability for the work.' A coded phase general, B during-work. It is a principle about authorship credit, not a step in a particular piece of work, so general (A). Both code P62 should-not and keep the fit note about accountability.

units.why: "does not directly address the use of GAI in generic courses" limits the scope of the section to dissertations and theses: P61.
units.anchor: The above guiding principle does not directly address the use of GAI in generic courses.
units.fit_note: Excludes ordinary courses and refers elsewhere, rather than defining AI. | States what the policy does not cover and refers to OFE and DELTA pages for courses.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A='admin' B='all'). Source: 'The above guiding principle does not directly address the use of GAI in generic courses.' A coded actor admin, B all. This is a statement of scope that applies to everyone reading the policy, not a rule binding a university office, so all (B). Both code P61 informs and keep the fit note about referring to other pages for courses.

units.why: "writing assistance tools such as Grammarly is generally allowed and rarely acknowledged" permits writing tools without disclosure (P18).
units.anchor: The use of writing assistance tools such as Grammarly is generally allowed and rarely acknowledged.

units.why: "If in doubt, students should contact their advisory committee and/or err on the side of caution and acknowledge use" is an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: If in doubt, students should contact their advisory committee
units.fit_note: Also says to acknowledge use when in doubt.

units.why: "legislating all this to the n-th degree will not be possible because of the constant evolution of the tools" acknowledges the policy cannot be exhaustive (P54).
units.anchor: legislating all this to the n-th degree will not be possible
units.fit_note: Cites tool evolution and calls for judgment; no review schedule. | Does not promise a review cycle; says the rules cannot be complete and judgment is needed.

units.why: "Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is the broad category of AI capable of generating new data" defines GAI (P61).
units.anchor: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is the broad category of AI capable of generating new data

units.why: "Large Language Models (LLM) are a subset of GAI" defines LLMs (P61).
units.anchor: Large Language Models (LLM) are a subset of GAI

units.why: "Writing Assistant Tools are designed but not limited to checking spelling and grammar" defines the category exempted in practice (P61).
units.anchor: Writing Assistant Tools are designed but not limited to checking spelling and grammar

units.why: "A clear and thorough description of whether and how tools from Generative Artificial Intelligence were used" is a required part of the Authorship Statement (P24).
units.anchor: A clear and thorough description of whether and how tools from Generative Artificial Intelligence were
units.fit_note: Delivered as part of the Authorship Statement, which the advisory committee must approve. | Places the AI disclosure in the required Authorship Statement of the thesis.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A='during-work' B='during-assessment'). Source: 'A clear and thorough description of whether and how tools from Generative Artificial Intelligence were used' (required content of the Authorship Statement). A coded during-work, B during-assessment. The statement is written into the thesis while the candidate is producing it, and the exam only approves it, so during-work. Both code P24 must require.

units.why: "Approval of the Authorship Statement by the advisory committee is a necessary condition for passing the final oral examination" makes the AI description reviewable by the committee; no disclosure type covers committee approval, so P62.
units.anchor: Approval of the Authorship Statement by the advisory committee is a necessary condition for passing
units.policy: Approval of the Authorship Statement, which includes the description of generative AI use, by the advisory committee is a necessary condition for passing the final oral examination.
units.fit_note: The statement includes the AI-use description; the rule does not mention AI by name.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: 'Approval of the Authorship Statement by the advisory committee is a necessary condition for passing the final oral examination.' Only B coded this. The Authorship Statement includes the required description of GAI use, so this is the enforcement of the disclosure rule and is kept; the normalized policy states the link to the AI description explicitly because the anchor does not name AI.
